content:
Iowa Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession: What Owners Should Know

Cash Home Buyers in Iowa
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Inherited, behind on payments, tenants, repairs: we buy it as-is
  • Zero fees, zero commissions, zero closing costs
  • No obligation: turn the offer down and owe us nothing

Selling a Iowa House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is. Tell us about the property and the timeline.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Iowa statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we do not state it.

Iowa law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Actions brought for the recovery of real property must be commenced within ten years (the limitation underlying Iowa adverse possession). (Iowa Code 614.1 (recovery of real property, 10 years); source)
  • Trespass includes entering or remaining on property without justification after being notified orally or in writing, or by conspicuously posted notice, to abstain or vacate by the owner or person in lawful possession. (Iowa Code 716.7(2)(a)(2); source)
  • Summary forcible entry and detainer remedy is available where a defendant entered by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth upon another's prior actual possession and detains it; also for holdover, lease breach, nonpayment of rent, and possession after a valid tax deed. (Iowa Code 648.1; source)
  • Thirty days' peaceable possession with the plaintiff's knowledge after the cause of action accrues bars the forcible entry and detainer proceeding. (Iowa Code 648.18; source)
Selling in Iowa?
We buy Iowa houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Details we could not confirm on an official page are not stated here. Read the statute sections linked above for the full text, and confirm deadlines with the court or county office.

How to sell a Iowa house when this applies to you

  1. Write down who is in the house and on what terms: owner, heirs, tenants or occupants with no lease.
  2. Ask the title company what it needs to insure the sale, such as a recorded deed, court papers or a payoff letter.
  3. Get the payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the proceeds at closing.
  4. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs. If you want a fast, simple closing, ask for a written cash offer. See we buy houses in Iowa.

What a cash sale of a Iowa house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Iowa.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Iowa disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Iowa

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Iowa change, so confirm details with the official office or a Iowa attorney or tax professional.

More questions about selling in Iowa

How fast can I close on a cash sale?

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs to clear ownership and payoffs.

Do I have to clean out or repair the house?

No. We buy houses as-is, so you do not need to make repairs before selling.

Will you buy a house that has tenants in it?

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate is finished?

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

Is there any cost to request an offer?

No. Requesting an offer is free and carries no obligation.

Iowa Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Iowa house?

Only by meeting every requirement of the adverse possession statute cited above for the full period. Check the statute and talk to a Iowa attorney about your facts.

Can I sell a house that has squatters in it?

Yes. We buy houses as-is, including occupied ones. Tell us who is in the property when you request an offer.

Should I remove a squatter myself?

No. Use the legal process described in the official sources above. Self-help removal can create liability for the owner.

  • Month-to-month tenancy may be terminated by either party by written notice at least thirty days before the periodic rental date specified in the notice (week-to-week: ten days). (Iowa Code 562A.34(1)-(2); source)
  • Landlord must give at least 24 hours' notice of intent to enter and enter at reasonable times, except in emergency or if impracticable; tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for inspection, repairs, or showings to purchasers. (Iowa Code 562A.19; source)
  • Landlord must comply with housing codes affecting health and safety, make repairs to keep the premises fit and habitable, and maintain electrical, plumbing, heating and other supplied facilities. (Iowa Code 562A.15(1); source)
  • Retaliation by raising rent, cutting services, or threatening an action for possession after a tenant's code complaint, complaint under 562A.15, or tenant union activity is prohibited; a good-faith complaint within one year creates a presumption of retaliation; tenant may recover damages and attorney fees.   • No-cause end of month-to-month tenancy: 30 days' written notice; holdover tenants may be sued for possession and, if willful and not in good faith, for actual damages and attorney fees. (Iowa Code 562A.34(2), (4); source)

content:
Iowa Tax Deed and Tax Lien Sales: Process, Redemption and Selling First

Cash Home Buyers in Iowa
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Inherited, behind on payments, tenants, repairs: we buy it as-is
  • Zero fees, zero commissions, zero closing costs
  • No obligation: turn the offer down and owe us nothing

Selling a Iowa House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is. Tell us about the property and the timeline.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Iowa statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we do not state it.

When property tax goes unpaid in Iowa, the statutes allow the taxing authority to sell a lien or the property itself, and they give the owner a set time to redeem. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Iowa sells tax sale certificates (liens) of purchase, with a deed available only after the redemption period; if no bid is received or the bid is below the amount due, the county treasurer bids the total amount due for the county. (Iowa Code 446.19(1); source)
  • A parcel sold at tax sale may be redeemed by paying the county treasurer the sale amount plus certificate fee and interest of two percent per month (each fraction of a month counted as a full month), plus later-year payments with interest. (Iowa Code 447.1(1); source)
  • After one year and nine months from sale (nine months for sales under 446.18; three months for 446.19A/446.19B), the certificate holder may serve notice that the right of redemption expires and a deed will issue unless redeemed within ninety days of completed service. (Iowa Code 447.9(1); source)
  • The county may redeem owner-occupied residential parcels for owners unable to contribute to public revenue, on petition to the board of supervisors. (Iowa Code 447.9(3); source)
  • A summary forcible entry and detainer remedy is available against defendants who remain in possession after issuance of a valid tax deed. (Iowa Code 648.1(6); source)
